summary: This memo states the requirements for establishing a new Domain and introduces the limited set of top-level domains. It is an official policy statement of the IAB and DARPA.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 920 sets out early rules for creating and managing domains in the ARPA-Internet. It names an initial set of top-level domains and explains how administrators should register and operate domains.

subtitle: A 1984 policy memo on domain administration and the initial top-level domains.

tldr.problem: The early domain name system needed rules for assigning responsibility for names and for establishing domains beneath the top level.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines administrative responsibilities, service and registration expectations, and an initial set of top-level domain categories.
tldr.outcome: RFC 920 is an October 1984 policy statement that planned for the ARPA top-level domain to be temporary and described domain changes expected at that time.

today: RFC 920 is a policy statement published in October 1984, and the unit metadata lists its status as Unknown. The memo describes plans and requirements from that time and does not state what later happened to them.

sections.title: Domains as Administrative Units
sections.content:
RFC 920 restates and expands the requirements for establishing a domain first described in RFC 881. It describes domains as administrative entities that divide responsibility for managing names and related information, rather than as groups defined by geography, technology, or common hardware.

The domain name space is a tree. Top-level domains contain second-level domains, which may contain further levels. Administrators control names within their domain and provide access to names and related information.
sections.plainLanguage: A domain assigns responsibility for managing a group of names to an administrator. Domains can be divided into smaller domains, forming a tree of delegated responsibility.

sections.title: The Initial Top-Level Names
sections.content:
The initial set included ARPA as a temporary domain, plus GOV, EDU, COM, MIL, and ORG for broad categories. The memo also allowed two-letter country codes and proposed that a large international multiorganization might qualify as a top-level domain when it did not fit the categories.

The RFC states that no country or multiorganization domains had yet been established. Its university and consortium examples are explicitly described as fictional examples created by the authors.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo proposed broad top-level names for government, education, commercial, military, and other organizations. It also provided for country codes and certain international groups.

sections.title: Administrative and Service Requirements
sections.content:
A domain needed a responsible person with authority and technical ability to address problems. It also needed a robust name service; one suggested way was to operate at least two independent servers without a shared point of failure. A domain could cooperate with another domain or arrange for a third party to operate its service.

The memo gave a general guideline of over 500 hosts for authorizing a top-level domain and over 50 hosts for a second-level domain, while calling the second-level threshold very soft. A domain administrator registered with the administrator of the level above, who checked whether the requirements were met.
sections.plainLanguage: A domain needed a responsible administrator, reliable name servers, and registration with the level above it. The memo gave size guidelines but allowed flexibility for major organizations.

sections.title: Registering a Domain
sections.content:
The NIC Domain Registrar asked for the top-level domain to join, administrative and technical contacts, the proposed domain name, and details of the name servers. The registration also included estimated host counts at the start and at one, two, and five years.

The memo specified that the proposed domain name in this registration form could be up to 12 characters. It described this as a prototype of the questions the registrar might ask, and said the questions could change.
sections.plainLanguage: To request a domain, an organization submitted contacts, server information, its proposed name, and estimates of its size. The RFC presented these questions as a prototype for the registrar's process.

sections.title: Planned Changes to ARPA Names
sections.content:
The memo describes ARPA as a temporary top-level domain and says the plan was for it to end as soon as possible. Existing hosts were advised to choose another domain. DDN hosts that did not join the domain system would continue to use the NIC-maintained HOSTS.TXT file, while their names were expected to change on a schedule set by DDN-PMO.

Because the domain is part of a host name, changing domains changes the name and can make older references outdated. The memo advises hosts and domain administrators to agree on membership and to consider the effects of renaming.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo expected hosts to move away from the temporary ARPA domain. It warned that changing a domain also changes a host's name and can leave old references out of date.
